plan.contextChunk: This figure shows the logistic sigmoid function sig[z] plotted as a single smooth curve over the range z ∈ [−5, 5]. The horizontal axis is labeled z with tick marks at −5.0, 0.0, and 5.0, and the vertical axis is labeled sig[z] with tick marks at 0.0 and 1.0. A smooth orange S-shaped curve rises monotonically from near zero on the left to near one on the right, with its steepest slope occurring at z = 0 where the function equals exactly 0.5. Gray dashed lines indicate the horizontal asymptote at sig[z] = 1.0 and mark a vertical reference at z = 0, emphasizing the function’s symmetry and its asymptotic approach to both bounds. This figure introduces the logistic sigmoid as a differentiable, bounded activation function that squashes any real-valued input into the interval (0, 1), motivating its use for modeling probabilities in binary classification.

interactionPlan.concept: The logistic sigmoid squashes any real-valued input z into the open interval (0,1), rising smoothly and monotonically through 0.5 at z = 0, which lets a real-valued score be read as a probability.
elements: Rectangular plot frame with black border on white background
Horizontal axis labeled 'z' with ticks at -5.0, 0.0, 5.0
Vertical axis labeled 'sig[z]' with ticks at 0.0 and 1.0
Smooth orange S-shaped sigmoid curve, thick stroke, spanning z ∈ [-5, 5]
Formula annotation 1 / (1 + exp[-z]) typeset as a fraction near the top-center of the plot
Light gray dotted horizontal guide from the y-axis at sig[z] = 0.5 to the curve
Light gray dotted vertical guide from z = 0 up to the curve at 0.5
Draggable marker dot on the curve with a coordinate readout label (z, sig[z])
Adjustable horizontal threshold line with value label
Vertical drop line at the z-value where the curve crosses the threshold, labeled z*
Optional shaded decision regions: 'predict 0' left of z*, 'predict 1' right of z*
Faint dotted asymptote lines at sig[z] = 0 and sig[z] = 1

interactions.teaches: That every input z maps to exactly one output strictly between 0 and 1 — huge negative z gives almost 0, huge positive z gives almost 1, and the output changes fastest near z = 0.

interactions.label: Probability threshold
interactions.teaches: That choosing a probability cutoff is equivalent to choosing a cutoff z* on the raw score, and that shifting the threshold slides the decision boundary along z.

interactions.label: Show decision regions
interactions.teaches: That the sigmoid plus a threshold partitions the whole real line into a 'class 0' and a 'class 1' half, which is what makes it usable for binary classification.

demo_steps.title: A curve with two ceilings
demo_steps.narration: The orange curve never touches 0 or 1 but approaches both. Drag the marker toward either edge and watch the output flatten out — large-magnitude scores barely change the probability.

demo_steps.title: The centre point
demo_steps.narration: At z = 0 the sigmoid passes through exactly 0.5, where the curve is steepest. This is the point of maximum sensitivity: small changes in the score move the probability the most.

demo_steps.title: A threshold is a cutoff in z
demo_steps.narration: The horizontal line marks a probability cutoff; where it meets the curve defines z*. At 0.5 the cutoff sits at z* = 0 — the natural, symmetric decision boundary.

demo_steps.title: Raising the bar
demo_steps.narration: Demand 90% confidence and z* slides far to the right: far fewer inputs are classified as class 1. Lower the threshold and the boundary slides left.

demo_steps.title: Lowering the bar
demo_steps.narration: At a 0.2 threshold almost any mildly positive score is labelled class 1. The curve is unchanged — only where we cut it has moved.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The sigmoid does not decide anything — it just compresses an unbounded score into (0,1); the decision comes from where you cut the curve, and a probability threshold is nothing more than a disguised threshold on z.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Single-panel line plot inside a heavy black rectangular frame, white background, generous margins. x-axis spans -5 to 5 with labelled ticks only at -5.0, 0.0, 5.0 (plus small unlabelled minor ticks); y-axis spans 0 to 1 with labelled ticks only at 0.0 and 1.0, label 'sig[z]' rotated vertically, serif/math-style typography throughout. The sigmoid is a thick (~4px) muted terracotta-orange line, smooth, flat near y=0 at the left edge, steepest at the origin, flattening near y=1 at the right edge. Centered near the top of the plot area sits the formula 1/(1+exp[-z]) rendered as a stacked fraction with a horizontal rule. Faint gray dotted guides run horizontally from the y-axis to the curve at y=0.5 and vertically from the x-axis at z=0 up to that intersection. Interactive additions: a filled orange draggable dot on the curve with a small boxed readout showing 'z = …, sig[z] = …'; a dashed slate-blue horizontal threshold line across the plot with its value labelled at the right; a dashed vertical drop from the crossing point to the x-axis labelled z*. When decision regions are on, shade the region left of z* in pale blue ('predict 0') and right of z* in pale orange ('predict 1') with small legend text at the bottom corners.

discrepancies: An orange filled marker dot sits at (0, 0.5) in the default state; the source curve has no point marker, so the step-0 view is not a pure drop-in replacement for the static image.

Axis-label typography is smaller relative to the plot than in the source: the source's 'sig[z]', 'z', '1.0', '0.0', '-5.0', '5.0' are large and bold-feeling, while the generated ones read as small secondary text, weakening the label hierarchy.
Plot aspect ratio is closer to square than the source's wide (≈3:2) frame, making the sigmoid appear steeper through the origin than in the original.
The dotted guide lines are drawn with a much finer dash/lighter weight than the source's clearly visible grey dotted guides, so they are faint at inline size.
evaluation.notes: A faithful, well-composed reproduction of the logistic sigmoid with correct curve shape, boxed frame, tick marks, guide lines and the fraction formula, backed by genuinely useful interactions (threshold slider, decision-region toggle, 5-step narrated demo, draggable marker); main weaknesses are the extra marker dot in the default state, undersized axis-label typography, and a squarer aspect than the source.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are concrete implementation details (hide default marker, enlarge axis-label typography, widen aspect ratio, strengthen dotted guides) best fixed in generation.
